column2: Which transaction gives a manufacturer new capital in exchange for a stake in its business?
column7: Subscribers pay the company for an ownership interest. Selling existing shares transfers ownership between investors.

column2: A pension fund buys newly issued corporate bonds. What is its relationship to the issuer?
column7: Each bond represents money owed by the issuer. Owning it does not give the pension fund a share of the business.

column2: Which market lets a UK wholesaler buy yen to settle a supplier's invoice?
column7: The wholesaler needs one currency in exchange for another. Borrowing sterling would still leave the invoice payable in yen.

column2: What is created when a bank grants a new loan by crediting the customer's current account?
column7: The deposit is spendable money. The borrower also has a liability for the same amount, so the loan itself creates no net wealth.

column2: Which asset do UK banks transfer between their Bank of England accounts to settle payments?
column7: Balances at the central bank are reserves. A customer's deposit is a liability of their own commercial bank.

column2: Which resource absorbs losses when borrowers default on loans made by a bank?
column7: Capital provides a cushion against credit losses. Deposits are amounts the bank owes its customers.

column2: Which payment does an investor receive at maturity on a conventional gilt bought below par?
column3: Nominal value plus the final coupon
column4: Purchase price plus the final coupon
column5: Market value on the purchase date
column7: The issuer redeems the gilt at face value and pays the last instalment of interest. An investor's purchase price does not change either payment.

column2: A saver owns £5,000 nominal of a conventional 4% gilt. What is each full half-year coupon?
column7: Annual interest is 4% of £5,000, or £200. Two equal payments divide that amount in half.

column2: Which index determines the inflation adjustment on UK index-linked gilt payments?
column7: The Debt Management Office uses the Retail Prices Index with a lag to adjust both coupon payments and the redemption amount.

column2: Which policy action illustrates quantitative easing by the Bank of England?
column7: Bond purchases raise bond prices and can bring down longer-term interest rates. A Bank Rate cut is a different monetary policy tool.

column2: How do higher interest rates normally affect the cost of borrowing and the incentive to save?
column3: Borrowing costs rise, saving grows more attractive
column4: Borrowing costs rise, saving grows less attractive
column5: Borrowing costs fall, saving grows more attractive
column6: Borrowing costs fall, saving grows less attractive
column7: Higher rates tend to raise loan costs and increase returns on savings. Both effects can reduce current spending.

column2: What does the Monetary Policy Committee primarily seek to stabilise through Bank Rate decisions?
column7: The committee sets monetary policy to meet the inflation target. Changes in borrowing or the exchange rate can transmit that policy.

column2: A tenant owes rent, catalogue instalments and credit card bills. Which arrears take priority?
column7: Housing arrears risk loss of the home. The consequences of non-payment determine priority before comparing interest rates.

column2: A client has no cash reserve. Where should money for unexpected bills normally be held?
column7: An emergency fund needs to be available when the expense arises. Locking the money away or exposing it to market falls can defeat that purpose.

column2: Mia borrows £1,200 on a credit card to buy shares now worth £900. Before interest or repayments, what does she owe?
column7: The card balance is the amount borrowed. The £300 market loss reduces the value of Mia's shares and leaves the debt outstanding.

column2: What happens to the capital on a repayment mortgage if every scheduled payment is made?
column3: It reduces to zero at term
column4: It is all due at maturity
column5: It falls only when rates rise
column6: It is paid by the linked insurer
column7: The instalments cover interest and part of the capital. Interest-only instalments leave the original capital to be repaid separately.

column2: What must an interest-only borrower usually pay at maturity after meeting every scheduled interest payment?
column7: Regular payments service the interest. The borrower needs a separate means of repaying the outstanding capital.

column2: A mortgage tracks Bank Rate plus 1.4 points with no floor. Bank Rate is 3%. What rate applies?
column7: The contract adds the margin to the reference rate. The calculation is 3% plus 1.4 percentage points.

column2: Which mortgage deal removes uncertainty over the interest rate for the next three years?
column7: The rate stays at the agreed level throughout the fixed period. A discount on a variable rate can still change with the underlying rate.

column2: A borrower has reached the lender's standard variable rate. Who sets that rate?
column7: Each lender sets its own standard variable rate. A change in Bank Rate can influence the lender without dictating an identical change.

column2: Which life cover is designed to follow the falling balance of a repayment mortgage?
column7: The sum assured reduces during the term to reflect a falling loan balance. Level cover keeps a constant sum assured.

column2: Parents need a fixed death benefit until their child turns 21. Which policy fits?
column7: Level term cover pays the agreed sum on death within a defined period. The amount stays constant during that term.

column2: A client needs monthly payments if illness prevents them working. Which cover addresses that need?
column7: Income protection replaces a portion of earnings during qualifying incapacity. Critical illness cover generally pays a lump sum for a listed diagnosis.

column2: Sick pay lasts 26 weeks. Which income protection term lets payments start after that interval?
column7: The deferred period is the wait before benefit starts for a qualifying claim. The maximum claim period governs how long payments can continue.

column2: Which benefit usually pays a lump sum on diagnosis of a specified serious illness?
column7: The illness must satisfy the policy's definition. The trigger is a covered diagnosis rather than an ongoing loss of earnings.

column2: Which change reduces an investor's exposure to the fortunes of one British retailer?
column4: Use a second broker for its stock
column7: Diversification changes the underlying exposures. Using several accounts to hold the same shares leaves the business risk unchanged.

column2: An investor sells shares at a gain inside a stocks and shares ISA. How is the gain treated for UK tax?
column7: Capital gains on investments held inside an ISA are exempt. The exemption does not depend on the investor having unused annual gains allowance.

column2: How should a taxpayer report cash ISA interest on their Self Assessment return?
column7: ISA interest is tax-free and does not need to be declared on the return.

column2: Which workplace pension promises benefits under a formula using earnings and years of service?
column7: A defined benefit scheme sets the income by its rules. A money purchase scheme builds a pot whose value depends on contributions and investment performance.

column2: Two employees contribute alike to money purchase pensions. What could produce different pot values?
column7: Money purchase contributions are invested. Performance and charges can change the amount available at retirement.

column2: Which retirement arrangement leaves capital invested and lets the saver vary withdrawals?
column7: Drawdown leaves the fund exposed to returns and gives the saver control over withdrawals. The income can fall or the pot can run out.

column2: Which retirement product promises payments until death, even if the buyer outlives their life expectancy?
column7: A lifetime annuity pays for as long as the annuitant lives. A fixed-term annuity can end while the buyer is still alive, and a drawdown fund can run out.

column2: Which record principally determines an individual's entitlement to the new State Pension?
column7: Qualifying years on the National Insurance record determine entitlement. Private pension balances do not purchase those qualifying years.

column2: A homeowner gives away her house but continues living there alone rent-free. How is it normally treated for Inheritance Tax?
column7: She has kept a benefit from the gift. Giving away legal title alone does not remove the house from her estate for this purpose.

column2: Which detail should a donor record alongside the date and recipient of a lifetime gift?
column4: Value at the next tax year end
column7: The estate representative needs to know what was given, to whom, when and its value at the time of the gift.

column2: A client wants life cover to pay whenever death occurs. Which policy meets that need if premiums continue?
column7: Whole-of-life cover has no fixed expiry date. A term policy only covers death within its term.

column2: A director signs a loan solely for her limited company without a guarantee. Who owes the lender?
column7: The company has a legal identity separate from its directors and owners. Signing for the company does not itself give a personal guarantee.

column2: A remittance firm authorises a shop to contract on its behalf. Which party is the principal?
column7: The principal gives the authority. The shop is the agent exercising it in dealings with customers.

column2: What standard does the Consumer Rights Act imply when a trader supplies a service to a consumer?
column7: The Act treats the service contract as including a duty to exercise reasonable care and skill. A particular outcome is a different promise.

column2: In England, a welfare LPA withholds authority over life support. Who normally decides on life-sustaining treatment after capacity is lost?
column7: Where the donor withholds this authority, doctors normally decide about life-sustaining treatment. Other welfare decisions depend on the terms of the LPA.

column2: In Wales, a capable donor permits immediate use of a financial LPA. When can the attorney first act under it?
column7: A property and financial affairs lasting power of attorney must be registered. Where its terms allow use while the donor has capacity, the donor must also give permission.

column2: Who can create a lasting power of attorney for an adult in England?
column7: Making an LPA requires the donor to understand the decision when they make it. Family relationship cannot substitute for that capacity.

column2: Two friends hold a home as beneficial joint tenants. One dies leaving everything to charity. Who takes the home?
column7: Survivorship passes the beneficial ownership to the other joint tenant. The deceased cannot direct that interest elsewhere by will.

column2: Co-owners want unequal beneficial shares that each can leave by will. Which arrangement fits?
column7: Tenants in common can hold different shares and dispose of them by will. Beneficial joint tenants have equal rights to the whole.

column2: An undischarged bankrupt wants to act as a company director. Whose permission is required?
column7: Bankruptcy restrictions prevent the individual acting as a director without permission from the court. Shareholder approval cannot lift the restriction.

column2: A bankrupt individual trades under a new business name. What must customers also be told?
column7: The person must disclose the name under which they were made bankrupt when doing business under another name.

column2: In England, a testator signed an ordinary will alone. How must they acknowledge their signature?
column7: A testator can sign, or acknowledge an existing signature, in the presence of at least two witnesses at the same time. Each witness must also sign or acknowledge their signature in the testator's presence.

column2: In Wales, a will leaves a painting to one of its two attesting witnesses. What follows?
column7: A gift to an attesting witness is void. The witness can still give evidence of execution and the other gifts can take effect.

column2: What can an adult beneficiary of an English bare trust demand if absolutely entitled?
column7: In a bare trust the trustee holds title, but the adult beneficiary has the right to the entire fund.

column2: A trust gives Arun its net income for life and leaves the capital to another beneficiary. What does Arun hold?
column7: Arun has a present right to income as it arises. The trust keeps the underlying capital for the other beneficiary.

column2: Who chooses which eligible family member receives a payment under a discretionary trust, within its terms?
column7: The deed gives trustees discretion over distributions among the eligible beneficiaries. Membership of the class creates no fixed right to a particular payment.

column2: What distinguishes an accumulation trust's handling of undistributed income?
column3: It may be added to capital
column4: It passes to a life tenant
column6: It belongs to the trustees personally
column7: The trustees can retain income and add it to the trust capital. An immediate income entitlement would require distribution instead.
